subject: Maths
chapter: Chapter 5: Tales by Dots and Lines
central_question: How do mean, median, dot plots, spreadsheets and line graphs help us describe the centre of data, analyse changes and draw meaningful conclusions?
in_scope_units: The mean as a balancing centre on a dot plot.
Equal total distances on the two sides of the mean.
How inserting, removing, increasing or decreasing data values affects the mean.
How adding a constant to all values or multiplying all values changes the mean.
The median and its behaviour when data values are inserted or removed.
Finding missing values and correcting a mean when data are changed.
Mean and median from frequency tables.
Spreadsheet tables, cells, ranges and formulae such as SUM and AVERAGE.
Line graphs for representing change over time.
Reading, comparing and interpreting multiple line graphs.
Generating questions and observations from temperature, rainfall, sunrise, sunset, moonrise and moonset data.
The closing Game of Hex strategy activity.
banned_topics: Regression, correlation coefficients and trend-line equations.
Database programming beyond the spreadsheet operations shown in the chapter.

known_pitfalls.claim: The mean is always the midpoint of the smallest and largest values.
known_pitfalls.correction: The mean balances the total distances on its two sides; it is not generally the midpoint of the extremes.

known_pitfalls.claim: Adding one value above the old mean leaves the mean unchanged.
known_pitfalls.correction: Adding a value above the current mean increases the mean; a value below it decreases the mean.

known_pitfalls.claim: The median of an even number of values is either one of the two middle values.
known_pitfalls.correction: It is the arithmetic mean of the two middle values after sorting.

known_pitfalls.claim: The mean of a frequency table is the sum of distinct values divided by the number of distinct values.
known_pitfalls.correction: Each value must be multiplied by its frequency, and the total divided by the sum of frequencies.

known_pitfalls.claim: A line graph alone proves why a change occurred.
known_pitfalls.correction: A graph shows patterns and changes; explanations of causes need additional evidence.

recommended_example_progression: Use the opening dot plots for 3 and 7, and 8 and 9, to show the mean halfway between two values.
Use the balancing-distance activity to show equal total distances on both sides of a mean.
Use the chapter's wrestler-weight missing-value problem whose unknown value is 43.
Use the family-size frequency table to calculate mean 188/36 = 5.22 and median 5.
Use the student-marks spreadsheet to demonstrate SUM and AVERAGE formulae and copying formulae.
Use one of the final line-graph activities to identify axes, read approximate values and distinguish observations from unsupported causes.
ncert_end_of_chapter_exercises_reference: The chapter ends with an extended Figure it Out set of data and line-graph interpretation tasks, including sunrise-sunset and moonrise-moonset questions, followed by the Summary and Game of Hex.
